lead: The mass transfer coefficient k<sub>c</sub> (m/s) is measured for a given flow, but it is not a fluid property alone. Film, penetration and surface-renewal theories each explain k<sub>c</sub> by a simple picture of the fluid next to the interface. Film theory uses an equivalent stagnant thickness δ. Penetration theory uses a short exposure time t. Surface-renewal theory uses a fractional renewal rate s. Film theory makes k<sub>c</sub> proportional to the diffusivity D (m²/s); the other two make it proportional to √D. They guide absorber and packed-tower design, where liquid-film coefficients control transfer of sparingly soluble gases.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the definition of kc, and the topic of molecular diffusion for Fick's law and diffusion in a stagnant layer.

blocks.text: The film model imagines a stagnant layer of thickness δ next to the interface. The bulk fluid is well mixed, so its concentration C<sub>b</sub> is uniform up to the outer edge of the layer. Across the layer, mass moves by molecular diffusion only, and the concentration profile is taken as linear. Fick's law gives the flux as N<sub>A</sub> = (D/δ)(C<sub>b</sub> − C<sub>i</sub>). Comparing with N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub>(C<sub>b</sub> − C<sub>i</sub>) gives k<sub>c</sub> = D/δ. Here D is diffusivity (m²/s), δ is the equivalent film thickness (m), and k<sub>c</sub> is the mass transfer coefficient (m/s). The model is simple and fits two-resistance calculations, but δ is not a measured physical thickness. It is chosen so that D/δ matches an observed k<sub>c</sub>. The model predicts k<sub>c</sub> ∝ D: doubling D doubles k<sub>c</sub>. Real interfaces have eddies that penetrate close to the surface, so the true profile is curved and the film picture is approximate.

blocks.where: k<sub>c</sub> is the mass transfer coefficient (m/s); D is diffusivity (m²/s); δ is the equivalent film thickness (m).

blocks.text: Penetration theory treats contact as short and unsteady. An eddy brings fresh liquid to the interface. That element stays for an exposure time t (s), then mixes back into the bulk. During t, gas diffuses into a semi-infinite liquid. The average flux over the exposure gives N<sub>A</sub> = 2√(D/(πt))(C<sub>i</sub> − C<sub>0</sub>), where C<sub>0</sub> is the initial solute concentration in the liquid. Therefore k<sub>c</sub> = 2√(D/(πt)). The factor 2 comes from averaging over the exposure; the instantaneous value is √(D/(πt)). The model predicts k<sub>c</sub> ∝ √D. If D becomes four times larger, k<sub>c</sub> doubles. Penetration theory suits short-contact equipment: packed towers, falling films and bubbles. The exposure time is set by flow, not by a fitted film thickness. Its weakness is that all surface elements are given the same t, which is rarely true in a stirred vessel.

blocks.where: k<sub>c</sub> is the mass transfer coefficient (m/s); D is diffusivity (m²/s); t is exposure time (s); π is 3.1416.

blocks.text: Surface renewal theory removes the single exposure time. Fresh liquid reaches the surface at random times, so elements have a range of ages. Danckwerts defined s, the fractional surface renewal rate (s⁻¹). In a small time interval, a fraction s dt of the surface is replaced by fresh liquid. Integrating over all ages gives N<sub>A</sub> = √(D s)(C<sub>i</sub> − C<sub>0</sub>), so k<sub>c</sub> = √(D s). A large s means fast renewal and a large k<sub>c</sub>. The D dependence is again √D, not D. This single fact separates the film model from the other two. For a sparingly soluble gas in water, liquid-film resistance often controls, and measured k<sub>c</sub> values usually follow √D better than D. The reason is eddy diffusion near the interface: eddies carry solute close to the surface and make a fixed stagnant film unrealistic. Film theory remains useful as a limiting picture and as the basis of two-resistance design.

blocks.where: k<sub>c</sub> is the mass transfer coefficient (m/s); D is diffusivity (m²/s); s is the fractional surface renewal rate (s⁻¹).

blocks.text: Measured exponents of D usually fall between 0.5 and 1. Toor and Marchello's film-penetration model covers that range: surface elements that stay only briefly behave as in penetration theory (k<sub>c</sub> ∝ √D), while elements that stay long enough reach the steady linear profile of film theory (k<sub>c</sub> ∝ D).

figure.caption: The worked example. Each theory is fitted to the oxygen measurement, k<sub>L</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m/s at D = 2.1×10⁻⁹ m²/s, which fixes δ, t or s. The theories then part: for a solute with D = 1.2×10⁻⁹ m²/s film theory predicts 2.29×10⁻⁵ m/s, penetration and surface renewal 3.02×10⁻⁵ m/s.

spec.aria: Plot of liquid-film coefficient against diffusivity: a straight line through the origin for film theory and a square-root curve for penetration and surface renewal, both passing through the oxygen point 2.1e-9, 4.0e-5. At D 1.2e-9 they give 2.29e-5 and 3.02e-5. A panel lists the fitted film thickness 52.5 micrometres, exposure time 1.67 s and renewal rate 0.762 per second.

examples.question: Oxygen (D = 2.1×10⁻⁹ m²/s) is absorbed into water in a stirred vessel, and the measured liquid-film coefficient is k<sub>L</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m/s. (a) Fit each theory to this measurement: find the film thickness δ, the exposure time t and the renewal rate s. (b) Predict k<sub>L</sub> for a larger solute molecule with D = 1.2×10⁻⁹ m²/s in the same vessel and stirring.
steps: Film: k<sub>L</sub> = D/δ, so δ = D/k<sub>L</sub> = 2.1×10⁻⁹/4.0×10⁻⁵ = 5.25×10⁻⁵ m = 52.5 µm.
Penetration: k<sub>L</sub> = 2√(D/(πt)), so t = 4D/(π k<sub>L</sub>²) = 4 × 2.1×10⁻⁹/(π × 1.6×10⁻⁹) = 1.67 s.
Surface renewal: k<sub>L</sub> = √(D s), so s = k<sub>L</sub>²/D = 1.6×10⁻⁹/2.1×10⁻⁹ = 0.762 s⁻¹.
The flow is unchanged, so δ, t and s stay the same. Film: k<sub>L</sub> = 1.2×10⁻⁹/5.25×10⁻⁵ = 2.29×10⁻⁵ m/s.
Penetration: k<sub>L</sub> = 2√(1.2×10⁻⁹/(π × 1.67)) = 3.02×10⁻⁵ m/s. Surface renewal: k<sub>L</sub> = √(1.2×10⁻⁹ × 0.762) = 3.02×10⁻⁵ m/s.
Shortcut: penetration and renewal both give k<sub>L</sub> ∝ √D, so k<sub>L</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ × √(1.2/2.1) = 3.02×10⁻⁵ m/s; film gives 4.0×10⁻⁵ × 1.2/2.1 = 2.29×10⁻⁵ m/s.
examples.answer: δ = 52.5 µm, t = 1.67 s and s = 0.76 s⁻¹ all reproduce the oxygen measurement. For the second solute film theory predicts 2.3×10⁻⁵ m/s and the other two 3.0×10⁻⁵ m/s, a 32 % difference. Measuring the second solute is how the theories are told apart: one data point fits any of them.

traps: Treating δ as a real measured stagnant film. δ is an equivalent thickness chosen to match k<sub>c</sub>; it changes with flow and is not a property of the fluid.
A unit slip: δ in mm must be converted to m before D/δ. With D in m²/s, δ in m gives k<sub>c</sub> in m/s.
Using k<sub>c</sub> ∝ D for all data. Film theory doubles k<sub>c</sub> when D doubles; penetration and surface renewal increase it by only √2.
Omitting the factor 2 in penetration theory. The average flux over exposure time t has 2√(D/(πt)); dropping 2 halves the predicted k<sub>c</sub>.
Confusing surface renewal rate s with 1/t. In penetration theory t is a fixed exposure time; in surface renewal s is a random replacement rate.

quiz.q: Define δ in film theory and give its unit.
quiz.a: δ is the equivalent film thickness (m), selected so D/δ equals the measured k<sub>c</sub>. It is not necessarily a real stagnant layer thickness.

quiz.q: Why does film theory predict k<sub>c</sub> ∝ D while penetration theory predicts k<sub>c</sub> ∝ √D?
quiz.a: The film has a steady linear profile, so flux and k<sub>c</sub> are proportional to D/δ. Penetration has unsteady diffusion; penetration depth grows as √(Dt), so the average flux has √D. Surface renewal also averages over ages and gives √D.

quiz.q: For D = 1.5×10⁻⁹ m²/s and t = 0.8 s, find the penetration k<sub>c</sub>.
A film model has δ = 0.1 mm and D = 3×10⁻⁹ m²/s. Find k<sub>c</sub>.
Measured k<sub>c</sub> for a liquid rises by a factor 2 when D rises by 4. Which model is consistent: film, penetration or surface renewal? Explain.
quiz.a: Penetration or surface renewal is consistent. Both give k<sub>c</sub> ∝ √D, and √4 = 2. Film theory would give a factor 4 because it predicts k<sub>c</sub> ∝ D.

quiz.q: Write the surface-renewal formula and give the unit of s.
quiz.a: k<sub>c</sub> = √(D s). The fractional surface renewal rate s has unit s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why is a clean stagnant film a poor picture near a gas-liquid interface in a stirred tank?
quiz.a: Eddies reach close to the interface and renew the surface. The concentration profile becomes curved, and the effective film thickness changes with flow. δ is then an equivalent thickness, not a fixed physical layer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern design uses CFD with eddy diffusivity, and surface-renewal ideas appear in gas-liquid reactor models, bubble columns and bioreactors. Search terms are Higbie penetration theory, Danckwerts surface renewal and film theory mass transfer. Laboratory kc data from wetted-wall columns or stirred cells can test which model fits. For fast reactions, combine these pictures with the enhancement factor in Chapter 2.9.
